summary:
Catamarca is a province of Argentina and stands under the national framework set by Argentina's Gender Identity Law 26,743, which allows adults to change legal gender, image and birth name on civil registries without surgery, hormone therapy, a psychiatric diagnosis, or approval by a doctor or judge. No Catamarca-specific legal restriction or separate provincial gender-recognition procedure was identified in the sources, so the national pathway is what a visitor should expect to apply here.

The national framework binding every province has weakened in practice. The Washington Blade reported on 10 April 2025 that activists describe Argentina's trans community as being in a 'chaotic, desperate situation' under the Milei administration: the federal anti-discrimination agency INADI has been closed, the Women, Gender and Diversity Ministry eliminated, and trans people hired under the public-sector labour-inclusion quota dismissed in 2024. Violence, discrimination and poverty affecting trans people are reported to have worsened. Catamarca carries no separate reporting on how these national rollbacks are experienced locally, so the national picture stands as the baseline.

Nationally recorded violence bears directly on what a trans visitor in Catamarca should expect. The National LGBT+ Hate Crimes Observatory recorded at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity in 2025, a 62% increase year on year and the highest count in the observatory's ten years of operation, averaging one crime every 38 hours. Trans women and travestis made up 62.5% of victims (142 cases) and gay men 22% (50). The report ties the surge to institutional weakening and state legitimation of discriminatory discourse. These are national figures; no province-level breakdown for Catamarca was located, and raw national counts are not adjusted for population.

Argentina's Supreme Court left standing on 5 April 2025 the life sentence imposed on Gabriel Marino for the 2015 murder of trans activist Diana Sacayan, while rejecting attempts to reinstate the travesticidio aggravating circumstance removed by a cassation court in 2020, so the gender-motivated-crime aggravator is currently not applied in that case. Hate-crime data and this ruling indicate that legal protection against gender-motivated violence exists in statute but its application in practice is contested.
tangentialFactors:
Argentina's national anti-discrimination agency was abolished and shut down in February 2024 as a public-spending measure, and the Women, Gender and Diversity Ministry has been eliminated. Outright International's Argentina overview, updated 12 March 2026, records negative evaluations on same-sex relations, gender recognition and organisation registration, indicating deterioration in the country's overall standing on LGBTIQ+ rights.

In interviews in Buenos Aires on 4 April 2025, reported on 10 April 2025, trans activists including figures from organisations named for Diana Sacayan and for Lohana Berkins said the policies of the Milei administration had made the community more vulnerable to violence. Catamarca has no documented equivalent of this organised provincial advocacy or of a provincial monitoring body, so a visitor should not expect local civil-society infrastructure of the kind operating in the capital.
localsOnly:
Residents of Catamarca access legal gender change through the national civil registry under Law 26,743, without surgery, hormone therapy, psychiatric diagnosis, or judicial approval. Decree 476/2021 requires the national civil registry to offer a third gender marker X on national identity cards and passports, including for non-citizen permanent residents holding Argentine identity cards.

Law 26,743 grants adults access to sex reassignment surgery and hormone therapy through public and private health care plans, with equal access stated for non-binary, transgender and gender non-conforming persons. The February 2025 decree banning gender-affirming surgery and hormone therapy for persons under age 18 was ruled unconstitutional by a Federal Court in April 2025, restoring access nationwide. A second February 2025 decree governs the housing of transgender people in prisons; its operative terms are not provided by the sources.

Penal Code Article 80(4), as amended in 2012, imposes life imprisonment for homicide motivated by hatred based on gender identity or expression and on sexual orientation. As of 2019 no national law expressly addressed discrimination or harassment based on gender identity, and the national anti-discrimination agency was shut down in February 2024. Outright International records that anti-discrimination protections exist through national and provincial laws; whether Catamarca maintains a distinct provincial anti-discrimination instrument is not sourced here.

Consensual same-sex sexual activity has been lawful since 1887 under Law No. 1,920. Same-sex marriage has been legal since 15 July 2010 with the same benefits and protections as opposite-sex marriage, including adoption since July 2010, and the union convivencial under the Civil and Commercial Code has been available nationwide since 1 August 2015.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Catamarca-specific source was located in this inventory. The province's own enforcement practice, any provincial anti-discrimination or gender-identity instrument, provincial hate-crime counts, and local institutional capacity remain unresolved and not sourced. The national hate-crime figures cited are raw counts with no per-capita or population denominator, and no provincial breakdown was provided, so they cannot be read as a measure of risk in Catamarca relative to other provinces.

The operative terms of the February 2025 decree on housing transgender people in prisons are not provided by the sources and remain unresolved.
